1156.title: The lost son (Kern ch. 4)
1156.hook: a son who ran away returns as a poor laborer; his rich father slowly raises him until he can tell him the truth
1156.howItsDone: The parable of the lost son, told by the senior disciples in chapter four of the Lotus Sutra, is retold in East Asian Buddhist teaching as a picture of the Buddha's patient skillful means.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sariputra, who feared he'd been left out, was told by name that he would become a Buddha. Your line: he too will wake.

This time the Buddha isn't the one telling the story. In chapter four of the Lotus, the disciples stand up. They've just watched Sariputra receive his promise, and they're amazed, because they had stopped expecting anything more. Subhuti and Kasyapa are among them. They bow and say: let us tell you a story, to show what has happened to us. And the story is about a runaway.
screen: `THE DISCIPLES STAND UP.` → `LET US TELL YOU A STORY.` → `A STORY ABOUT A RUNAWAY.`

segments.voice: In Kern's telling, a young man leaves his father and wanders to other lands, growing poorer. Meanwhile his father searches for him, settles in a city, and grows very rich, with storehouses, servants and a crowd at his door. All the while he thinks of his son and tells no one. One day the son, now a beggar looking for work, drifts to his father's house. He sees a great man on a throne, surrounded by attendants, and doesn't recognize him. This must be a king, he thinks. If I stay, they'll seize me and force me to work. He runs. The father knows him at once and sends servants after him, and the son is so terrified he faints. So the father has water sprinkled on his face and lets him go, saying nothing. The father sends two men who look as poor as the son to offer him a job clearing away the dirt heap, for good wages. The son takes it. The father takes off his fine clothes and jewels, puts on dirty work clothes, picks up a basket, and works beside him. He talks to him, tells him to stay, raises his wages, starts calling him son. Even so, the son still thinks of himself as a hired hand. In time the father gives him charge of the whole household and its treasure, and still the son lives in his small hut. At last, near the end of his life, the father calls together his relatives, the king and the townspeople, and announces: this is my son, who ran away long ago. Everything I have is his. The father had the truth the whole time. What he waited for was a son who could hear it without running.

What do you have that you've never claimed? A skill you treat as a hobby. A family recipe nobody wrote down. A library card in a drawer. Things can be yours for years while you live as if they belong to someone else. In the Lotus, the disciples have just told of a son who swept the yard of a house that was his. Now they tell the Buddha who that son was, and it turns out they've been describing themselves the whole time.
screen: `WHAT HAVE YOU NEVER CLAIMED?` → `YOURS, BUT LIVED AS IF NOT.` → `THE SON WAS THEM.`

segments.voice: The disciples say: the rich man is the Buddha, and we are like his sons. Clearing the dirt heap was our practice of clearing away wrong views and bad states. It was real work, and it mattered. But we were content with the day's wage. The son was glad of his pay and asked for nothing more; in the same way the disciples had reached their own release, their own peace, and called it enough. They even taught the bodhisattvas about the Buddha's great knowledge, they say, without ever thinking it could be theirs, like the son put in charge of the treasure, who handled it every day and still slept in his hut. The Buddha knew our narrow wishes, they say, so he did not tell us everything at first. He worked beside us in plain clothes, so to speak, with teachings we could take in. That's skillful means from chapter two, seen from the receiving end. And now, in this sutra, the Buddha has called together the whole assembly and told us: you are my children, and what is mine is yours. In Kern's translation they describe it as a treasure that came to them without their seeking it. They hadn't asked for an inheritance. They hadn't known there was one. They were never really hired hands. They were heirs from the start. What changed was not what they owned, but that someone finally said it out loud, and they were ready to hear it. Tomorrow the Buddha answers them with a picture of his own, about rain.

1158.title: The rain on the plants (Kern ch. 5)
1158.hook: one rain falls on all plants, and each grows by its own nature
1158.howItsDone: The parable of the medicinal plants in chapter five of the Lotus Sutra is taught in East Asian Buddhism as a picture of the Buddha's equal compassion: one teaching, received differently by each person according to their capacity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the disciples saw they had been the Buddha's heirs from the start, working for a wage when the treasure was theirs. Your line: heirs all along.

A summer storm doesn't check the garden plan before it rains. The same water lands on the tomatoes, the weeds by the fence, the old maple and the moss between the paving stones. And the next morning each has done something different with it. The tomato swells. The maple pushes out new leaves. The moss turns bright green. In chapter five of the Lotus, the Buddha answers the disciples' story, and he chooses weather.
screen: `A STORM WITH NO GARDEN PLAN.` → `SAME WATER, EVERY PLANT.` → `THE BUDDHA ANSWERS WITH WEATHER.`

segments.voice: In Kern's translation the Buddha tells Kasyapa of a great cloud that rises and spreads over the whole world, covering everything. Then it rains, everywhere at once, on grasses, bushes, herbs and trees, small, middle-sized and large, on every growing thing on mountains, in valleys and on the plains. The rain doesn't choose. It is one rain, the sutra says, of a single taste. But each plant takes up the water by its own nature and size, and grows, flowers and bears fruit in its own way. A blade of grass doesn't become an oak. It becomes more fully grass. The Buddha says he is like that cloud. He appears in the world and teaches gods, humans and all beings alike, and his teaching has one taste: the taste of release. He doesn't hold some back and pour more on others. He is equal toward everyone, the noble and the poor, those who keep the rules and those who break them, the quick and the slow. The difference is in the receiving. Each hears the teaching by their own capacity, and grows from there. This fits the last few days. In chapter two the teaching took many shapes. Here the source of all those shapes is one. The many ways belong to the hearers, like the many plants. The one goal belongs to the rain. It doesn't ask the grass to be a tree, or the tree to apologize for being tall. It just keeps raining on everyone, and lets each grow toward the same light in the way only it can.

At a graduation, the names are read out one at a time. Each person waits for theirs. Some are calm. Some are gripping the arm of the chair. And between one name and the next, the people still waiting wonder if theirs is really on the list. Chapter six of the Lotus has that moment in it, except the list is of future Buddhas, and the ones waiting are some of the Buddha's closest disciples.
screen: `NAMES READ ONE AT A TIME.` → `GRIPPING THE CHAIR.` → `IS MY NAME ON THE LIST?`

segments.voice: Vyakarana is the Sanskrit word the Lotus uses for this kind of announcement: a prediction, a declaration, the Buddha saying out loud what someone's future will be. Sariputra received one in chapter three. Chapter six is named for it. The Buddha turns to Mahakasyapa, one of the disciples who told the story of the lost son, and declares that after honoring many Buddhas in ages to come, he will become a Buddha himself. Kern gives the name as Rasmiprabhasa, and the sutra describes his land: level, clean, with jeweled trees, free of rubble and thorns. Now the other great disciples, Subhuti, Katyayana and Maudgalyayana, are trembling. In Kern's translation they speak to the Buddha in verse, with a picture worth keeping. We are like a man who has come out of a famine, they say, and finds a royal meal set in front of him. He is starving, but he doesn't dare touch it until the king himself says: eat. They have heard that disciples can become Buddhas. They can't quite believe it applies to them until the Buddha says so by name. And the Buddha does. One by one he declares each a future Buddha, gives each a Buddha name, and describes each one's land and how long their teaching will last. The sutra takes its time over every one, as if no one should be hurried past. That is vyakarana in the Lotus. Not a horoscope about Tuesday. A teacher looking at a student and saying, in front of everyone: I see where you are going, and I am sure of it. The starving man is allowed to eat.

Chapter seven of the Lotus looks back, so far back that the sutra needs a whole picture just to say how long ago. The Diamond Sutra ground a world to dust to ask what a heap is. The Lotus grinds a world to dust to measure time. Carry the dust across the worlds, and let fall one speck only after crossing a great stretch of them, until the dust is gone. The time since this story is longer than that.
screen: `FROM FUTURES TO THE PAST.` → `DUST THAT MEASURES TIME.` → `LONGER AGO THAN THAT.`

segments.voice: Kern gives the old Buddha's name as Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu. He sat at the seat of awakening, and for a long time full awakening did not come. He stayed seated, steady, until at last it did. Before he left home, the story says, he had been a prince with sixteen sons. When they heard their father had awakened, they left their toys and palaces to honor him, their family following behind, and asked him to teach. Kings of the heavens came too, from every direction, offering their palaces and asking the same. Their father taught the early teachings first, and many were freed. Later the sixteen sons, now young monks, asked him for more, and he taught them this very sutra, the Lotus. Then he went into a long meditation, and while he sat, each son took a seat and taught the Lotus to the crowds, in detail, for a long time. Here is the turn. Those sixteen sons, the Buddha says, are all Buddhas now, teaching in different directions. One of them, in the west, is called Amitayus. And the sixteenth son is me. I am the one who taught you then. The listeners in front of him today are the same beings he taught as that young monk, ages ago. The long story isn't a detour. It tells the disciples why they are here. The teaching has a lineage older than they can picture, passed from father to sons, from sons to listeners, and they were already in it. Yesterday's promises weren't new. They were old seeds coming up.

Halfway up a hard trail, the group has stopped talking. Legs are shaking. Someone says what everyone is thinking: let's just go back down. And the trip leader says: there's a hut just past the next bend. They make it. They rest. And later, rested, they find the summit was closer than they thought. segments.voice: In Kern's translation the Buddha tells of a great crowd setting out across a wild and fearful forest, on a long road, to reach a place of treasure. Their guide is wise and knows every turn. But partway along the travelers are worn out and frightened. We can't go on, they say; let's turn back. The guide doesn't scold them. He is skilled in means, the sutra says, and he feels for them. So, by his own power, he makes a city appear in the middle of the wilderness. Look, he says, here is a city. Go in and rest. The travelers are delighted. They go in, rest, feel safe, and think they have arrived. When the guide sees they are rested, he makes the city vanish, and tells them: that city was something I made for you to rest in. The treasure is near. Come, let's go on. Then the Buddha explains. He is the guide, and the road is long and hard. If beings heard only about the far goal, Buddhahood, many would lose heart and turn back. So he teaches a resting place along the way: the peace, the release, the disciples have reached. It is real rest, given out of care. But it is not the end. The treasure, the Buddha's own awakening, is further on. Look at what the city is not. It isn't a trick to punish anyone, or a test. It's there because tired people need somewhere to sit down, and the guide stays with them the whole way. Carts, a dirt heap, rain, and now shelter: rest is part of the road.

1162.title: The jewel in the coat (Kern ch. 8)
1162.hook: a friend sews a jewel into a sleeping man's coat; he wanders poor for years without knowing
1162.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, the jewel in the coat is taught alongside the lost son and the phantom city as one of the sutra's parables about a gift already given and not yet recognized.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a worn-out caravan rested in a city their guide had conjured, and then he told them the treasure was further on. Your line: a city to rest in.

A coat hangs by the door. Stitched deep in the lining is a jewel worth more than its owner will earn this year. He wears that coat every day, counts his coins every week, and never finds it. That's almost the whole parable. What makes it strange is who tells it. In chapter eight of the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha has just promised a large company of monks that they too will one day be Buddhas. They don't answer with thanks. They answer with a story, and the story is about themselves.
screen: `A COAT BY THE DOOR.` → `A JEWEL IN THE LINING.` → `THE LISTENERS TELL THIS ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the story the monks tell. A man visits a friend who is well off. There's food and drink, and the man falls asleep. The friend has to leave on business before his guest wakes, so, as a parting gift, he sews a priceless jewel into the sleeping man's garment, and goes. The man wakes alone, wanders to another country, and scrapes by, working hard for food and clothes, satisfied with a little. Long after, the friend runs into him, astonished. Why are you living like this? I gave you a jewel. It's in your coat. Look. Then the monks say what it means. We were that man. Long ago the Buddha placed in us the aim of full awakening. We slept through it, found a small peace, and told ourselves it was the whole of it. Now he has shown us the lining. Notice the friend. He doesn't take the jewel back for being ignored, or wait for the man to deserve it. He just points. This is the week's last day, so look at the Lotus all week: a son who doesn't know he's the heir, travelers resting in a city that isn't the end of the road, a man poor with a fortune stitched into his clothes. Three stories, one turn: what the searcher wants has already been handed over. Some later teachers read the jewel as buddha-nature, already present in everyone, waiting to be noticed. The sutra keeps the picture simple: a coat, a lining, a friend who says look.

segments.voice: Be the friend in the story: bring to mind one person getting by on scraps, someone who doubts themselves or waves away what they're good at. Look for what's stitched into their lining, a steadiness, a kindness, a knack they never mention, and hold it the way you'd hold something you mean to hand back. If nothing comes, rest with the breath.
